**White Zimbabweans** (formerly **White Rhodesians**) are an [ethnocultural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnographic_group "Ethnographic group")[Southern African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_African "Southern African") people of [European](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europeans "Europeans") descent. Most are [English-speaking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English-speaking_world "English-speaking world") descendants of [British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire") settlers; a small minority are either [Afrikaans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afrikaans "Afrikaans")-speaking descendants of mostly [Dutch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_people "Dutch people") originating [Afrikaners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afrikaner "Afrikaner") from [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa") or descendants of [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greeks_in_Zimbabwe "Greeks in Zimbabwe"), [Irish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_people "Irish people"), [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_diaspora#The_Portuguese_diaspora "Portuguese diaspora"), [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Zimbabweans "Italian Zimbabweans"), and [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_Zimbabwe "History of the Jews in Zimbabwe") immigrants.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-Crush-2)

Following the establishment of the colony of [Southern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia "Southern Rhodesia") by Britain, white settlers began to move to the territory and slowly developed rural and urban communities. From 1923, the settlers concentrated on developing rich mineral resources and agricultural land in the area. In the aftermath of the Second World War, the number of white people emigrating to Rhodesia from Britain, Europe and other parts of Africa increased, almost doubling the white population, with white Rhodesians playing an integral role in the nation's strong economic development throughout the 1950s and early 1960s.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-8) At its height in the early 1970s, the number of white people in the region was the highest in Africa outside South Africa and Kenya, peaking at around 300,000 people, some 5% of the population.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-9)

Various social, economic and political disparities between the black majority and smaller white population were factors in the [Rhodesian Bush War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Bush_War "Rhodesian Bush War") after the government of white Prime Minister [Ian Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Smith "Ian Smith") implemented the [Unilateral Declaration of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence "Rhodesia's Unilateral Declaration of Independence"), establishing [Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia "Rhodesia") as a _de facto_ independent state in 1965, although it was not recognised internationally and was technically still a [British Colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Colony "British Colony"). Following the independence of Zimbabwe in 1980, the white population gradually began to decline; many remained in the country, with some still identifying as Rhodesian. White Zimbabweans continued to represent a majority of the country's middle and upper classes during the 1980s and 1990s, but after 2000 the population shrank further as a result of violence, economic instability and controversial land reform policies enacted by the government of [Robert Mugabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe "Robert Mugabe") in which white-owned farmland was forcibly seized.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-10)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-11) White Zimbabweans reportedly faced increased levels of poverty following the deterioration of the Zimbabwean economy during the 2000s and 2010s.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-12) An influx of returning White Zimbabweans, including farmers whose lands had been confiscated, followed Mugabe's removal from power and replacement by [Emmerson Mnangagwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmerson_Mnangagwa "Emmerson Mnangagwa").

Communities of White Zimbabweans continue to exist in larger towns and cities including [Bulawayo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulawayo "Bulawayo") and the [Harare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harare "Harare") metropolitan area, with numerous Harare suburbs such as [Avondale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avondale,_Harare "Avondale, Harare"), [Mount Pleasant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Pleasant,_Harare "Mount Pleasant, Harare") and [Borrowdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borrowdale_(Harare) "Borrowdale (Harare)") hosting significant white populations.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-16)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-17) According to the [2022 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Zimbabwe_census "2022 Zimbabwe census"), white Zimbabweans numbered just 24,888, representing 0.16% of the national population.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-zimstat_2022_PHC_Report_27012023_Final-1)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-18)

Present-day Zimbabwe (known as [Southern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia "Southern Rhodesia") from 1895) was occupied by the [British South Africa Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_South_Africa_Company "British South Africa Company") (BSAC) from the 1890s onward, following its subjugation of the [Matabele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ndebele_people "Northern Ndebele people") (Ndebele) and Shona nations. Early White settlers came in search of mineral resources, hoping to find a second gold-rich [Witwatersrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witwatersrand "Witwatersrand"). Zimbabwe lies on a plateau that varies in altitude between 900 and 1,500 m (2,950 and 4,900 ft) above sea level. This gives the area a moderate climate which was conducive to European settlement and commercial agriculture.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-19)

White settlers who assisted in the BSAC takeover of the country were given land grants of 1,200 hectares (3,000 acres); the native Black people who had long lived on the land were classified legally as tenants.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-20)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-21) In 1930, Land Apportionment and Tenure Acts displaced Africans from the country's best farmland, restricting them to unproductive and low-rainfall tribal-trust lands. It reserved areas of high rainfall for White ownership.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-22) White settlers were attracted to Rhodesia by the availability of tracts of prime farmland that could be purchased from the state at low cost. This resulted in the growth of commercial agriculture in the young colony. The White farm was typically a large (>100 km 2 (>38.6 mi 2)) mechanized estate, owned by a White family and employing hundreds of Black people. Many White farms provided housing, schools and clinics for Black employees and their families.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-23) At the time of independence in 1980, more than 40% of the country's farmed land was made up of approximately 5,000 White farms.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-24) At the time, agriculture provided 40% of the country's GDP and up to 60% of its foreign earnings.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-25) Major export products included tobacco, beef, sugar, cotton and maize. The minerals sector was also important. Gold, asbestos, nickel and chromium were mined by foreign-owned concerns such as [Lonrho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonmin "Lonmin") (Lonmin since 1999) and [Anglo American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo_American_plc "Anglo American plc").

The Census of 3 May 1921 found that Southern Rhodesia had a total population of 899,187, of whom 33,620 were Europeans; 1,998 were Coloured ([mixed race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed_race "Mixed race")); 1,250 Asiatics; 761,790 Bantu natives of Southern Rhodesia; and 100,529 Bantu aliens.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-26) The following year, Southern Rhodesians rejected, in [a referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesian_government_referendum,_1922 "Southern Rhodesian government referendum, 1922"), the option of becoming a province of the [Union of South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_of_South_Africa "Union of South Africa"). Instead, the country became a self-governing British colony. It never gained full [dominion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominion "Dominion") status, but unlike other colonies, it was treated as a _de facto_[dominion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominion "Dominion"), with its Prime Minister attending the [Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Nations "Commonwealth of Nations")[Prime Ministers' Conferences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Heads_of_Government_Meeting "Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting").

Portuguese explorer António Fernandes was the first European to visit the region.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-27)

In 1891, before Southern Rhodesia was established as a territory, it was estimated that about 1,500 Europeans resided there. This number grew slowly to around 75,000 in 1945. In the period 1945 to 1955, the White population doubled to 150,000, and during that decade 100,000 Black people were forcibly resettled from farmland designated for White ownership.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-28) However, some members of the White farming community opposed the forced removal of Black people from land designated for White ownership. Some favoured the transfer of underutilised "white land" to Black farmers. For example, in 1947, Wedza White farmer Harry Meade unsuccessfully opposed the eviction of his Black neighbour Solomon Ndawa from a 200-hectare (500-acre) irrigated wheat farm. Meade represented Ndawa at hearings of the Land Commission and attempted to protect Ndawa from abusive questioning.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-29)

[![Image 5: A woman playing golf while three men watch](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/2/2d/Wright07s.jpg/250px-Wright07s.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wright07s.jpg)

A Rhodesian couple plays golf, attended by their native caddies. Taken from a 1970 Rhodesian government booklet promoting White immigration, titled "The Good Life".

Large-scale migration to Rhodesia did not begin until after the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"). At the colony's first comprehensive census in 1962, Rhodesia had 221,000 White residents. At its peak in the mid-1970s, Rhodesia's White population consisted of as many as 277,000.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-30) There were influxes of White settlers from the 1940s through to the early 1970s. The country saw a net gain of 9,400 White immigrants in 1971, the highest number since 1957 and the third highest on record.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-31) In the immediate postwar period, the most conspicuous group were former British servicemen. However, many of the new immigrants were refugees from Communism in Europe; others were former service personnel from [British India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_India "British India"), or came from the former [Kenya Colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Colony "Kenya Colony"), the [Belgian Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgian_Congo "Belgian Congo"), Zambia, Algeria, and Mozambique. For a time, Rhodesia provided something of a haven for White people who were retreating from [decolonisation elsewhere in Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decolonisation_of_Africa "Decolonisation of Africa") and [Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decolonisation_of_Asia "Decolonisation of Asia").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-32) In 1974 the Smith government launched a massive campaign to attract one million Europeans to settle in the country.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-33)

Post-World War II Rhodesian White settlers were considered different in character from earlier Rhodesian settlers and those from other British colonies. In [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"), settlers were perceived to be drawn from "the officer class" and from the British [landowning class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landed_gentry "Landed gentry"). By contrast, settlers in Rhodesia after the Second World War were perceived as being drawn from lower social strata and were treated accordingly by the British authorities. As Peter Godwin wrote in _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_, "Foreign Office mandarins dismissed Rhodesians as lower middle class, no more than provincial clerks and artisans, the lowly NCOs of empire."[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-auto-34)

Various factors encouraged the growth of the White population of Rhodesia. These included the industrialisation and prosperity of the economy in the post-war period. The [National Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Party_(South_Africa) "National Party (South Africa)") victory in South Africa was one of the factors that led to the formation of the [Central African Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_African_Federation "Central African Federation") (1953–1963), so as to provide a bulwark against [Afrikaner nationalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afrikaner_nationalism "Afrikaner nationalism"). British settlement and investment boomed during the Federation years, as Southern Rhodesia, Northern Rhodesia (now Zambia), and Nyasaland (now Malawi) formed a powerful economic unit, counterbalancing the economic power of South Africa. The economic power of these three areas was a major factor in the establishment of the Federation through a British Act of Parliament. It was also apparent as early as the 1950s that [White rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_rule "White rule") would continue for longer in Rhodesia than it would in other British colonies such as Zambia (Northern Rhodesia) and Kenya. Many of the new immigrants had a "not here" attitude to majority rule and independence.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-35)

[![Image 6: A map of Zimbabwe shows land ownership in various colors representing European areas, Tribal Trust land, Native Purchase, and National land](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/61/Rhodesialand.png/330px-Rhodesialand.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rhodesialand.png)

Land apportionment in Rhodesia in 1965

Rhodesia was run by a White minority government. In 1965, that government declared itself independent through a [Unilateral Declaration of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence_(Rhodesia) "Unilateral Declaration of Independence (Rhodesia)") ('UDI') under Prime Minister [Ian Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Smith "Ian Smith").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-36) The UDI project eventually failed, after a period of [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") economic sanctions and a civil war known as the [Chimurenga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chimurenga "Chimurenga") (Shona) or [Bush War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Bush_War "Rhodesian Bush War"). British colonial rule returned in December 1979, when the country became the British Dependency of Southern Rhodesia. In April 1980, it was granted independence as [Zimbabwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe "Zimbabwe").

The Rhodesian community kept itself largely separate from the Black and Asian communities in the country.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-37) Urban Rhodesians lived in separate areas of town, and had their own segregated education, healthcare and recreational facilities. Marriage between black and white and Rhodesians was possible but rare, and interracial marriage remains to the present day very rare. The 1903 Immorality Suppression Ordinance made "illicit" (i.e. unmarried) sex between Black men and White women illegal – with a penalty of two years imprisonment for any offending White woman.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-38) The majority of the early White immigrants were men, and some White men entered into relationships with Black women. The result was a small number of mixed-race persons: 1,998 out of a total 899,187 inhabitants, according to the 1921 census, some of whom were accepted as being White. A proposal by [Garfield Todd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garfield_Todd "Garfield Todd") (Prime Minister in 1953–1958) to liberalise the laws regarding interracial sex was viewed as dangerously radical. The proposal was rejected and was one factor that led to the political demise of Todd.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-39)

White Rhodesians enjoyed a very high standard of living. The Land Tenure Act had reserved 30% of agricultural land for White ownership. Black labour costs were low (around US$40 per month in 1975) and included free housing, food and clothing. Nurses earned US$120 per month. The low wages had a large effect in the context of an agricultural economy.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-PTORW-40) Public spending on education, healthcare and other social services was heavily weighted towards white people. Most of the better paid jobs in public service were also reserved for White people.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-41) White people in skilled manual occupations enjoyed employment protection against Black competition.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-42) In 1975, the average annual income for a Rhodesian was around US$8,000 (equivalent to $47,000 in 2024) with income tax at a marginal rate of 5% — making them one of the richest communities in the world.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-PTORW-40)

In a [1922 referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1922_Southern_Rhodesian_government_referendum "1922 Southern Rhodesian government referendum"), the community rejected joining the [Union of South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_of_South_Africa "Union of South Africa"), electing instead to establish [responsible government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Responsible_government "Responsible government"). In the [1964 Rhodesian independence referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_Rhodesian_independence_referendum "1964 Rhodesian independence referendum"), the community voted overwhelmingly in favour of independence from Britain, leading to [Rhodesia's Unilateral Declaration of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence "Rhodesia's Unilateral Declaration of Independence") establishing the independent state of [Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia "Rhodesia") under Prime Minister [Ian Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Smith "Ian Smith"). Many white Rhodesians were concerned about the prospect of decolonization with majority rule due to conflicts that had taken place in other former British colonies such as the [Mau Mau rebellion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mau_Mau_rebellion "Mau Mau rebellion") in Kenya. Civil unrest had also occurred in other former European colonies such as the [Belgian Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgian_Congo "Belgian Congo") where the white population had been targets for violence and [Algeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algeria "Algeria") where [pieds-noirs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pieds-noirs "Pieds-noirs") settlers fled the country en-masse after independence.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-43)

Following the UDI, the white community was embroiled in the [Rhodesian Bush War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Bush_War "Rhodesian Bush War") (1964–1979), as the Smith government sought to maintain [White minority rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_minority_rule "White minority rule"). White men were conscripted into the [Rhodesian Security Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Security_Forces "Rhodesian Security Forces") and the [British South Africa Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_South_Africa_Police "British South Africa Police"). White civilians were targeted in some attacks such as [Air Rhodesia Flight 825](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Rhodesia_Flight_825 "Air Rhodesia Flight 825") and [Air Rhodesia Flight 827](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Rhodesia_Flight_827 "Air Rhodesia Flight 827").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-44)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-45)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-46) The community faced fresh economic challenges during the UDI period as Britain imposed economic sanctions and [Mozambique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mozambique "Mozambique") closed its border in 1976, blocking Rhodesia's access to the [Indian Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Ocean "Indian Ocean") and world commerce.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-47)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-48) Rhodesia was excluded from major sporting events, meaning that its White athletes were unable to participate in the [1968](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_Summer_Olympics "1968 Summer Olympics"), [1972](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Summer_Olympics "1972 Summer Olympics") and [1976](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_Summer_Olympics "1976 Summer Olympics")[Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-49)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-50)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-51)

A small number of British migrants had reached the [British colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Colonial_Empire "British Colonial Empire") of [Southern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia "Southern Rhodesia"), later Zimbabwe, as settlers during the late-nineteenth century. A steady migration of European peoples continued for the next 75 years. The White population of Southern Rhodesia, or Rhodesia as it was known from 1965, reached a peak of about 300,000 in 1975–76, representing around 8% of the population.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-52)

The country gained its independence as [Zimbabwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe "Zimbabwe") in April 1980, under a [ZANU-PF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ZANU-PF "ZANU-PF") government led by [Robert Mugabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe "Robert Mugabe"). Following independence, the country's White citizens lost most of their former privileges. A generous social welfare net (including both education and healthcare) that had supported Whites in Rhodesia disappeared almost in an instant. Whites in the artisan, skilled worker and supervisory classes began to experience job competition from Blacks. Indigenisation in the public services displaced many Whites. The result was that White emigration gathered pace. In the ten-year period from 1980 to 1990, approximately two-thirds of the White community left Zimbabwe.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-53) About 49% of emigrants left to settle in South Africa, many of whom were [Afrikaans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afrikaans "Afrikaans") speakers, with 29% going to the [British Isles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Isles "British Isles"); most of the remainder went to Australia, New Zealand, Canada, Hong Kong and the United States.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-54) Many of these emigrants, as well as some who remained, continued to identify themselves as [Rhodesian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia "Rhodesia").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-:2-55)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-56) A White Rhodesian or Zimbabwean who is [nostalgic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nostalgia "Nostalgia") for the UDI era is known colloquially as a "[Rhodie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodie "Rhodie")".[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-:2-55) These nostalgic "Rhodesians" are also sometimes referred to by the pejorative "[Whenwes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whenwe "Whenwe")", coming from the phrase "when we were in Rhodesia" and have been characterised by popular culture as has having a strong sense of loss and nostalgia for their former country.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-New_Internationalist-57)

However, many Whites resolved to stay in the new Zimbabwe; only one-third of the White farming community left. An even smaller proportion of White urban business owners and members of the professional classes left. Although White Zimbabweans had lost their advantageous position in society after 1980, the lifting of economic sanctions against Zimbabwe allowed middle class whites to generate more wealth and opportunities.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-58) This pattern of emigration meant that although small in absolute numbers, Zimbabwe's White population remained a high proportion of the upper strata of society. A 1984 article in _[The Sunday Times Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Sunday\_Times\_Magazine "The Sunday Times Magazine")_ by White Zimbabwean author [Peter Godwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Godwin "Peter Godwin") described and pictured the life of Zimbabwean White people at a time when their number was just about to fall below 100,000. Godwin wrote that by this time Zimbabwean whites in the cities generally lived a comfortable lifestyle but had retreated from public life while those in the countryside still remained wary of the new government.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-59)

The 1979 [Lancaster House Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster_House_Agreement "Lancaster House Agreement"), which was the basis for independence from the United Kingdom, had precluded compulsory land redistribution in favour of subsidised voluntary sale of land by White owners for a period of at least 10 years. The pattern of land ownership established during the Rhodesian state therefore survived for some time after independence. Those White people who were prepared to adapt to the situation they found themselves in were therefore able to continue enjoying a very comfortable existence. In fact, the independence settlement, combined with favourable economic conditions (including the Economic Structural Adjustment Programme), produced a 20-year period of unprecedented prosperity for White Zimbabwean people, and for the White farming community in particular; a new class of "young White millionaires" appeared in the farming sector.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-60) These were typically young Zimbabweans who had applied skills learned in agricultural colleges and business schools in Europe. In 1989, [Commercial Farmers' Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_Farmers%27_Union "Commercial Farmers' Union") president John Brown commented, "This is the best government for commercial farmers that this country has ever seen".[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-61)

The lifting of UN-imposed economic sanctions and the end of the [Bush War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Bush_War "Rhodesian Bush War") at the time of independence produced an immediate 'peace dividend'. Renewed access to world capital markets made it possible to finance major new infrastructure developments in transport and schools. One area of economic growth was tourism, catering in particular to visitors from Europe and North America. Many White people found work in this sector. Another area of growth was horticulture, involving the cultivation of flowers, fruits and vegetables, which were air-freighted to market in Europe. Many White farmers were involved in this, and in 2002 it was claimed that 8% of horticultural imports into Europe were sourced in Zimbabwe.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-62) The [economic migrant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_migrant "Economic migrant") element among the White population had departed quickly after independence, leaving behind those White people with deeper roots in the country. The country settled and the White population stabilised.

Chris McGreal, writing in _[The Observer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Observer "The Observer")_ in April 2008, claimed that before the political and economic situation in Zimbabwe deteriorated, Zimbabwe's White people "... kept their houses and their pools and their servants. The White farmers had it even better. With crop prices soaring they bought boats on Lake Kariba and built air strips on their farms for newly acquired planes. Zimbabwe's Whites reached an implicit understanding with Zanu-PF; they could go on as before, so long as they kept out of politics".[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-63)

White Zimbabweans with professional skills were readily accepted in the new order. For example, Chris Andersen had been the hardline Rhodesian justice minister, but made a new career for himself as an independent MP and leading attorney in Zimbabwe. In 1998, he defended former President [Canaan Banana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canaan_Banana "Canaan Banana") in the infamous "sodomy trial".[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-64) At the time of this trial, Andersen spoke out against the attitude of President Mugabe who had described homosexuals as being "worse than dogs and pigs since they are a colonial invention, unknown in African tradition."[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-65)

[John Bredenkamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bredenkamp "John Bredenkamp") started his trading business during the UDI era, when he developed expertise in "sanctions busting". He is reported to have arranged the export of Rhodesian tobacco and the import of components (including parts and munitions for the Rhodesian government's force of Hunter jets) in the face of UN trade sanctions. Bredenkamp was able to continue and expand his business after independence, making himself a personal fortune estimated at US$1 billion.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-66)

Several White Zimbabwean businessmen, such as [Billy Rautenbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Rautenbach "Billy Rautenbach"), have returned to Zimbabwe after working abroad for some years. Rautenbach has succeeded in extending Zimbabwean minerals sector activity into neighbouring countries such as the [Democratic Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo "Democratic Republic of the Congo").[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-67) Charles Davy is one of the largest private landowners in Zimbabwe. Davy is reported to own 1,200 km 2 (460 mi 2) of land, including farms at Ripple Creek, Driehoek, Dyer's Ranch and Mlelesi. His property has been almost unaffected by any form of land redistribution, and he denies that this fact has any link to his business relationship with the politician [Webster Shamu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Webster_Shamu "Webster Shamu"). Davy has said about Shamu, "I am in partnership with a person who I personally like and get along with".[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-68) Other views on Shamu are less kind.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-69)

The political environment in Zimbabwe has allowed the development of an exploitative business culture, in which some White businessmen have played a prominent role.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-70)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-71) When Zimbabwe was subject to EU sanctions, arising from its involvement in the DRC from 1998, the government was able to call on sanctions-busting expertise and personnel from the UDI era to provide parts and munitions for its force of Hawk jets. After 25 years of ZANU-PF government, Zimbabwe had become a congenial place for White millionaires of a certain kind to live and do business in.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-TheZimbabwean-72)

The Independence constitution contained a provision requiring the Zimbabwean government to honour pension obligations due to former servants of the Rhodesian state. This obligation included payment in foreign currency to pensioners living outside Zimbabwe (almost all White). Pension payments were made until the 1990s, but they then became erratic and stopped altogether in 2003.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-73)

Following the land invasions and chaotic political situation in the country, a number of expatriate White farmers and hoteliers from Zimbabwe resettled in neighbouring [Zambia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambia "Zambia"), where they were reviving agriculture and developing the local tourism industry.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-74)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-75) In 2009, the British government commenced a [repatriation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repatriation "Repatriation") plan assisting elderly British citizens living in Zimbabwe to resettle in the United Kingdom.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-76)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-77) Challenges for some of Zimbabwe's remaining White community included being reliant on remittances sent by relatives overseas, the cost of private healthcare and the cost of living.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-78)

#### Lancaster Deal and Land reform

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=White_Zimbabweans&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Lancaster Deal and Land reform")]

The Lancaster house agreement took place from 10 September – 15 December 1979 with 47 [plenary sessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plenary_session "Plenary session") formally held in which [Lord Carrington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Carington,_6th_Baron_Carrington "Peter Carington, 6th Baron Carrington"), [Foreign and Commonwealth Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Foreign_and_Commonwealth_Affairs "Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs") of the United Kingdom, chaired the Conference.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The content of Lancaster House Agreement covered the [new constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Zimbabwe "Constitution of Zimbabwe"), pre-independence arrangements, and the terms of ceasefire along with an agreement of a bilateral payment from the UK to the republic of Zimbabwe in aid to the land reforms. The agreement signed under Margaret Thatcher, sought out to aid the oncoming land redistribution as powers shifted from the known Rhodesia to the now known Zimbabwe.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

By the mid-1990s, it is thought that around 120,000 White people remained in Zimbabwe.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-79) In spite of this small number, the White Zimbabwean minority maintained control of much of the economy through its investment in commercial farms, industry, and tourism. However, an ongoing programme of [land reforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_reform_in_Zimbabwe "Land reform in Zimbabwe") (intended to alter the ethnic balance of land ownership) dislodged many White farmers. The level of violence associated with these reforms in some rural areas made the position of the wider White community uncomfortable. Twenty years after independence, there were 21,000 commercial farmers in the country.

In 1997, the British prime minister Tony Blair and his government pulled out of talks to fund the Lancaster House agreements causing a traction. This would lead to the land grabs that were seen soon after. The war veterans felt as if the inability of the UK government to continue its agreement meant they must take a stand. The land grabs formally followed after, in cause of the crumbling relations with the UK government.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The Fast track land reform came to assume a very high profile in Zimbabwe's political life. ZANU politicians sought to revise Rhodesian land apportionment, which they saw as an injustice and pressed for land to be properly dispersed among White and Black ownership. White farmers argued that this served little purpose. Therefore, to their eyes, the problem was really a lack of development, rather than one of land tenure. White farmers would respond to claims that they owned "70% of the best arable land" by stating that what they actually owned was "70% of the best developed arable land", and therefore that the two are entirely different things.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-80) Whatever the merits of the arguments, in the post-independence period, the land issue assumed enormous symbolic importance to all concerned. As the euphoria of independence subsided, and as a variety of economic and social problems became evident in the late-1990s, the land issue became a focus for trouble.

The intention was to equally allocate the 4,000 White-owned farms, covering 110,000 km 2 (42,470 mi 2) of mostly prime farmland, among the native Black majority. The means used to implement the programme were ad-hoc, and involved forcible seizure in many cases.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-81)

By March 2000, little land had been redistributed as per the land reform laws that were passed in 1979, when the [Lancaster House Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster_House_Agreement "Lancaster House Agreement") between Britain and Zimbabwe pledged to initiate a fairer distribution of land between the White minority, which governed Zimbabwe from 1890 to 1979, and the native Black population.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] However, at this stage, land acquisition could only occur on a voluntary basis. Little land had been redistributed, and frustrated groups of government supporters began seizing White-owned farms. Most of the seizures took place in [Nyamandlovu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyamandhlovu "Nyamandhlovu") and [Inyati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inyati "Inyati").[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-82)

By mid-2006, only 500 of the original 5,000 White farms were still fully operational.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-83) The majority of the White farms that avoided expropriation were in Manicaland and Midlands, where it proved possible to do local deals and form strategic partnerships. However, by early-2007, a number of the seized farms were being leased back to their former White owners (although in reduced size or on a contract basis); it has been claimed to be possible that as many as 1,000 of them could be operational again, in some form.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-84)

A [University of Zimbabwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Zimbabwe "University of Zimbabwe")[sociologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociologist "Sociologist") told [IWPR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_for_War_and_Peace_Reporting "Institute for War and Peace Reporting") journalist Benedict Unendoro that the _[esprit de corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esprit\_de\_corps "Esprit de corps")_ of the White dominant class in the former [Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia "Rhodesia") prevented the poor White people from becoming a recognisable social group, because of the social assistance provided by the dominant social class on racial grounds. This system broke down after the founding of Zimbabwe, causing the number of poor White people to increase, especially after 2000, when the confiscation of White-owned farms took its toll. As rich White land owners emigrated or fended for themselves financially, their White employees, who mainly worked as supervisors of Black labour, found themselves destitute on the streets of cities like Harare, with many found begging around urban centres like Eastlea. The land confiscated from White owners was redistributed to Black peasant farmers and smallholders, acquired by commercial land companies, or persons connected to the government.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-85)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-86)

Sympathisers of the expropriated White farmers claimed that lack of professional management skills among the new landholders resulted in a dramatic decline in Zimbabwe's agricultural production.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-87) In an effort to boost their own agricultural output, neighbouring countries, including Mozambique and Zambia, offered land and other incentives to entice Zimbabwe's White farmers to emigrate.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-88)

By 2008, an estimated one in ten out of 5,000 White farmers remained on their original farmland; many of these continued to face intimidation.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-89) By June 2008, _[The Daily Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Daily\_Telegraph "The Daily Telegraph")_ reported that 280 White farmers remained in Zimbabwe, and all of their farms were "invade[d]".[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-90) On the day of Mugabe's inauguration as president on 28 June 2008, several White farmers who had protested the seizure of farm land were beaten and burned by his supporters.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 2017, new President Emmerson Mnangagwa's inaugural speech promised to pay compensation to the White farmers whose land was seized during the land reform programme.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-91) Rob Smart became the first White farmer whose land was returned within a month after President Mnangagwa was sworn in to office; he returned to his farm in Manicaland province by military escort.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-92) During the [World Economic Forum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Economic_Forum "World Economic Forum") 2018 in [Davos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davos,_Switzerland "Davos, Switzerland"), Mnangagwa also stated that his new government believes thinking about racial lines in farming and land ownership is "outdated", and should be a "philosophy of the past." There were thought to be around 300-400 white farmers left in the country, down from 4,000 prior to Mugabe's land reforms eighteen years prior.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-:4-93) Hundreds of White farmers returned to Zimbabwe following a mellowing of government restrictions on White Zimbabweans owning land, with many of the returning White farmers forming joint ventures with Black farmowners.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-:3-94)

Ahead of the Ahead of the [2018 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Zimbabwean_general_election "2018 Zimbabwean general election"), Mnangagwa held a public meeting for an audience of White Zimbabweans in Borrowdale, Harare in which conceded that many white farms which had been seized under land reform programmes had gone to government officials, soldiers and tribal chiefs who did not know much about farming, before asking whites to work with his government.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-:5-95)

> I know of some chiefs who have moved from one farm to another. Then they run it down. Then he leaves that farm and he is issued another one. He runs it down. That time is gone.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-:5-95)

The speech both drew mixed responses among opposition politicians and was seen by commentators as a shift from Mugabe's policies and an attempt to court white voters.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-:5-95)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-96)

By September 2023, there were thought to be as many as 900 White-run commercial farms in the country. The farmers were not usually working their own land, but were renting in joint ventures from Black farmers given confiscated White-owned land.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-:3-94)

Government compensation payments to white farmers who were expelled from their properties under Mugabe began in 2025. Payments cover improvements which they made on the land, rather than the land itself.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-:1-97)

Since the 2000s, there has been a surge in violence against Zimbabwe's white population. The main targets of this violence has often been white farmers, with both human rights groups and journalists documenting reports of White Zimbabwean farmers and their families being victims of murder, threats of violence, property destruction and forced evictions. Violent incidents and racially motivated attacks against whites have also been reported in cities and towns.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-98)[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-99)[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-100)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-101)

Much of the violence against White Zimbabwean farmers was initiated after a proposal on fast-tracking land reform policies was put forward by Mugabe's government during the late 1990s and early 2000s. This led to subsequent protests organised by the pro-Mugabe [Zimbabwe National Liberation War Veterans Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_National_Liberation_War_Veterans_Association "Zimbabwe National Liberation War Veterans Association") (ZNLWVA) calling for land transfers to Black Zimbabwean war veterans which spilled into invasions of white-owned farms and physical attacks on white farmers. Black Zimbabwean militant groups and mobs began to systematically harass white farmers whilst assaulting and sometimes killing Black Zimbabwean agricultural workers on their properties. In 2000, militants shot dead a white farmer David Stevens at his home in the first documented case of a murder since the land reform programme was pushed by Zimbabwe's government.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-102)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-Hughes2010-103) In 2001, it was reported that nine white farmers had been killed and in September of that year the [Commercial Farmers' Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_Farmers%27_Union "Commercial Farmers' Union") said that least 829 "violent or hostile" incidents had taken place on commercial farms. In August 2001, Zimbabwe police reported that a violent mob had swept through [Chinhoyi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinhoyi "Chinhoyi") assaulting and injuring White Zimbabweans in the street and in a supermarket.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-104)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-105)

In 2002, [Human Rights Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Rights_Watch "Human Rights Watch") documented that at least seven White Zimbabwean farmers had been killed along with black farm workers.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-106)

In April 2008, a fresh round of invasions of white owned farms was reported with white farmers allegedly being forced out of their homes with threats of punishment. Hendrik Olivier, the then director of the Commercial Farmers Union accused both the Zimbabwean police of being complicit in allowing the attacks to happen and the state owned [Zimbabwe Broadcasting Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_Broadcasting_Corporation "Zimbabwe Broadcasting Corporation") of encouraging violence against white farmers.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-107)

In June 2008, a British-born farmer, [Ben Freeth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Freeth "Ben Freeth"), who had published several articles and letters in the British press allegeding hostility against White farmers, and his in-laws, Mike and Angela Campbell, were abducted and found badly beaten.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-108)[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-109)[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-110) Campbell, speaking from hospital in Harare, vowed to continue with his legal fight for his farm.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-111) In November 2008, a [SADC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_African_Development_Community "Southern African Development Community") tribunal ruled that the Zimbabwean government had racially discriminated against Campbell, denied him legal redress, and prevented him from defending his farm.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-112)

On 18 September 2010, droves of White Zimbabweans were chased away and prevented from participating in the constitutional outreach programme in [Harare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harare "Harare") during a weekend, in which violence and confusion marred the process, with similar incidents having occurred in the Harare suburb of Graniteside. In [Mount Pleasant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Pleasant,_Harare "Mount Pleasant, Harare"), white families were subjected to a torrent of abuse by suspected [ZANU-PF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ZANU%E2%80%93PF "ZANU–PF") supporters, who later drove them away and shouted racial slurs.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-113)

After the beating to death of a prominent white farmer in September 2011 near Harare, the head of the [Commercial Farmers' Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_Farmers%27_Union "Commercial Farmers' Union") Charles Taffs decried the attack, saying that its white members continued to be targeted with violence without protection from the government.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-114) The Commercial Farmers' Union also rejected a report from the police which claimed the farmer was killed during a robbery and argued it was part of a recent pattern of political violence and that the authorities were deliberately failing to arrest and prosecute those behind the attacks.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-115)

In 2012, [Genocide Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genocide_Watch "Genocide Watch") declared that the violence against Whites in Zimbabwe was a stage 5 (of [10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ten_stages_of_genocide "Ten stages of genocide")) case of [genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genocide "Genocide").[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-116)

Violence and intimidation against the white community has also spilled into suburban and urban districts and whites have been the target of a degrading campaign by the Zimbabwean State media throughout the 2000s. Several state newspapers referred to White Zimbabweans as "Britain's Children" and "settlers and colonialists".[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-117)[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing\_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_] In 2006,[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-118)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-119) Several White Zimbabweans living in the affluent Harare suburb of [Borrowdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borrowdale,_Harare "Borrowdale, Harare") were evicted from their homes because of their proximity to Mugabe's new home in the area. In April 2007,[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-120) it was reported that 100 mostly white youths were arrested during a police paramilitary raid at Borrowdale's Glow nightclub, before being transported in two police buses and detained in the downtown central police station. In a statement, the Zimbabwean police said that the raid was part of a crackdown on underage drinking in bars and beer halls, although eyewitnesses reported that several of the youths were beaten by police while others among the detainees said they witnessed white females being separated into different groups where they were threatened with rifles, slapped by police officers and denied phone calls to relatives after the raid.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-121)[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-122)

In September 2014, Mugabe publicly declared that all White Zimbabweans should "go back to England", and urged Black Zimbabweans not to lease agricultural land to White farmers.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-123)

In August 2017, Mugabe declared that people who had murdered white farmers would not face prosecution. That same year, he also encouraged Zimbabwean youths at a government rally to forcibly occupy white farms in [Mashonaland East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mashonaland_East "Mashonaland East") and drive the farmers away.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-124)

Prominent White Zimbabwean opposition politicians such as [Roy Bennett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Bennett_(politician) "Roy Bennett (politician)") and [David Coltart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Coltart "David Coltart") have been targets of racially motivated threats and electoral violence.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-TheZimbabwean-72)[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-125)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-126)

More recently, international commentators have noted that the Zimbabwean government under Emmerson Mnangagwa has softened its attitude to White Zimbabweans and attempted to court support among the white community. After coming to power, Mnangagwa said he would financially compensate white farmers whose land had been confiscated by the state and claimed he would no longer address land reform policy through racial lines, describing it as an "outdated" practice.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-:1-97)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-:4-93) Compensation payments began in 2025.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-127)

[![Image 7: Bar plot shows the differences between exports and imports of the United States from 1965 to 1979](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/Net_migration_of_white_people_from_Rhodesia_between_1965_and_1979.png/250px-Net_migration_of_white_people_from_Rhodesia_between_1965_and_1979.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Net_migration_of_white_people_from_Rhodesia_between_1965_and_1979.png)

Net migration of white people from Rhodesia between 1965 and 1979

Emigration after the country gained internationally recognised independence as Zimbabwe in 1980 resulted in a declining White population: estimated at 220,000 in 1980; 70,000 in 2000;[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-128) and 30,000 in 2012.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-129)[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-130) However, by 2023, the White population had increased following the government easing restrictions regarding White ownership of farmland. Many formerly dispossessed White farmers have formed joint ventures with Black landowners.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-:3-94) White ministers in the [Zimbabwean Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwean_Government "Zimbabwean Government") have included [Kirsty Coventry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirsty_Coventry "Kirsty Coventry"), [Joshua Sacco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Sacco "Joshua Sacco") and [Vangelis Haritatos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vangelis_Haritatos "Vangelis Haritatos").[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-131)[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-132)[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-133) In 2023, [David Coltart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Coltart "David Coltart") was elected as [Mayor of Bulawayo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_Bulawayo "Mayor of Bulawayo").[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-134)

In November 1965, in order to avoid the introduction of Black majority rule (commonly referred to at the time as the [Wind of Change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_of_Change_(speech) "Wind of Change (speech)")), the Government of what was then the [self-governing colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-governing_colony "Self-governing colony") of [Southern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia "Southern Rhodesia") issued the [Unilateral Declaration of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence "Rhodesia's Unilateral Declaration of Independence") (UDI), upon which the country became the _de facto_ independent – albeit [unrecognised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_states_with_limited_recognition "List of states with limited recognition") — state of [Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia "Rhodesia").

As was the case in most European colonies, White settlers took a privileged position in all areas of society. Extensive areas of prime farmland were owned by Whites. Senior positions in the public services were reserved for Whites, and Whites working in manual occupations enjoyed legal protection against job competition from Black Africans. As time passed, this situation became increasingly unwelcome to the majority ethnic groups within the country and also to wide sections of international opinion, leading to the [Rhodesian Bush War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Bush_War "Rhodesian Bush War") and eventually the [Lancaster House Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster_House_Agreement "Lancaster House Agreement") in 1979.

After the country's [reconstitution](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/reconstitute "wikt:reconstitute") as the Republic of Zimbabwe in 1980, White Zimbabweans had to adjust to being an ethnic minority in a country with a Black majority government. Although a significant number of White Zimbabweans remained, many of them emigrated in the early-1980s, both in fear for their lives and an uncertain future. Political unrest and the seizure of many white-owned commercial farms resulted in a further exodus of White Zimbabweans commencing in 1999. The 2002 census recorded 46,743 White Zimbabweans living in Zimbabwe. More than 10,000 were elderly and fewer than 9,000 were under the age of 15.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-135)

At the time of Zimbabwean independence in 1980, it was estimated that around 38% of White Zimbabweans were UK-born, with slightly fewer born in Rhodesia, and around 20% from elsewhere in Africa.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-136) The White population of that era contained a large transient element, and many White people might better be considered foreign migrants than settlers.[_[original research?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:No\_original\_research "Wikipedia:No original research")_][_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Between 1960 and 1979, White emigration to Rhodesia was around 180,000, while white emigration overseas was 202,000 (with an average White population of around 240,000).[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-137)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:NOTRS "Wikipedia:NOTRS")_] White emigration accelerated as independence approached. In October 1978 the net White emigration of 1,582 was the highest recorded number of departures since Rhodesia declared its UDI in 1965. According to official government statistics, 1,834 Whites emigrated and 252 White immigrants arrived.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-138) In the first nine months of 1978, 11,241 Whites emigrated.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-139) In an attempt to stem emigration, the Rhodesian government allowed each departing family to only take up to $1,400 out of the country.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-140)

After Mugabe was removed as President and replaced by Emmerson Mnangagwa, some White Zimbabweans returned. By September 2023, there were thought to be as many as 900 farms run by Whites, most of them in joint ventures with Blacks who had been given the properties after government confiscation.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-:3-94) In 2025, the ruling party ZANU-PF boasted that significant numbers of Whites were returning to the country; they constituted the largest group of returning Zimbabweans.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-141)
