In addition to the dominant [Anglo-Celtic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Celtic "Anglo-Celtic") population, other White communities exist in Zimbabwe.

The first wave of Afrikaners arrived in ox wagons in 1893, brought to the country at the time by the pioneer Duncan Moodie.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-sparks-151) The Afrikaners that followed mostly settled on farms in the subtropical lowlands of the southeast, and on the high central and northwestern plains known for its [cattle ranching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cattle_ranching "Cattle ranching"). It is estimated that the community peaked in the late 1960s, numbering some 25,000.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-sparks-151)[P. K. van der Byl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P._K._van_der_Byl "P. K. van der Byl"), an Afrikaner, served as Rhodesia's [Minister of Foreign Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Foreign_Affairs_(Zimbabwe) "Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Zimbabwe)") (1974–1979).[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-152) Thousands returned to South Africa after independence in Zimbabwe in 1980; however, as many as 15,000 remained four years later in 1984.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-sparks-151) They were sometimes disparaged by their Anglo-Saxon counterparts in the country, who referred to them as "japies", "hairy-backs", "rock spiders" and "ropes".[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-153)[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-154) Until the end of the Second World War, "the race problem" in Southern Rhodesia referred exclusively to Afrikaner and English-speaking rivalries.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-chennells-155) However, Afrikaners in the country did not push for the most radical demands of [Afrikaner nationalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afrikaner_nationalism "Afrikaner nationalism"), including the absolute rejection of empire.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-chennells-155) "Anti-Dutch" sentiment contributed to White Rhodesia's rejection of union with South Africa in the 1922 referendum, as well as a fear that union would bring a wave of Afrikaner "poor Whites" to the country.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-chennells-155) Some Afrikaners came to the country to escape the [National Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Party_(South_Africa) "National Party (South Africa)") politics, and they looked to Southern Rhodesia, not to become closer to Britain, but to forge a White African identity with English-speaking Whites that was free of the Afrikaner supremacy in South Africa.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-chennells-155)

The earlier wave of Jewish immigration consisted of [Ashkenazi Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashkenazi_Jews "Ashkenazi Jews") from [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia") and [Lithuania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithuania "Lithuania").[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-jp-156) An active Jewish community with a synagogue has existed in Salisbury (now Harare) since 1894.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-bloom-157) In the 1930s, a wave of [Sephardi Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sephardi_Jews "Sephardi Jews") arrived from [Rhodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodes "Rhodes"), the Greek island. [German Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Jews "German Jews") fleeing persecution in the [Third Reich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Reich "Third Reich") also settled in the country.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-jp-156) A number of Jews arrived from the [Belgian Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgian_Congo "Belgian Congo"), escaping the civil war engulfing the newly independent country.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-jp-156) The Jewish community reached a peak of 7,060 to 7, 500 between 1961 and the early 1970s.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-jp-156)[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-bloom-157) There were three active synagogues in Salisbury (now Harare), one in [Bulawayo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulawayo "Bulawayo") and a plethora of Jewish community centers, sports clubs, primary schools, youth movements and other organizations, such as the _[Chevra Kadisha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chevra\_Kadisha "Chevra Kadisha")_ (Jewish burial society). Smaller Jewish communities also existed in [Gatooma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gatooma "Gatooma"), [Gwelo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gwelo "Gwelo") and [Que Que](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Que_Que "Que Que").[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-bloom-157) There are currently two active synagogues in the country, both are in [Harare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harare "Harare"): the Ashkenazi synagogue and the Sephardi synagogue. As congregation numbers have depleted, both communities combine [minyanim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minyanim "Minyanim") on [Shabbat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shabbat "Shabbat").[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-bloom-157) Two Jewish primary schools continue to operate, with Sharon School in Harare, and Carmel in [Bulawayo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulawayo "Bulawayo"). With the local Jewish community decreasing in size, most of the students at the schools are not Jewish, however.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-158)

The Greek Community in Zimbabwe peaked at between 13,000 and 15,000 people in 1972, but has decreased significantly to around 1,000 Greeks or people of Greek origin.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-mfagreece-159) The Greek Cypriot community in Zimbabwe is slightly larger, with 1,200 Cypriots continuing to live in the country.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-mfagreece-159) The Greeks and Cypriots were mostly known for running restaurants and small businesses in the country.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-nyt1965-160) There are some significant Greek and Cypriot business owners and landowners, with the majority of the Hellenic community employed in trade professions or involved in bakery operations.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-mfagreece-159)[Hellenic Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellenic_Academy "Hellenic Academy"), an independent Greek high school, was established in [Harare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harare "Harare") in 2008.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-mfagreece-159) The Holy Archdiocese of Zimbabwe and Southern Africa is under the jurisdiction of the Patriarchate of Alexandria.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-mfagreece-159)

Italians came to Zimbabwe as early as 1906, when they formed a settlement named Sinoa in today's [Chinhoyi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinhoyi "Chinhoyi").[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-1R-161)

Portuguese migrants came from [Portuguese Mozambique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Mozambique "Portuguese Mozambique") to work in the building trade,[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-nyt1965-160) with later waves coming from newly independent [Angola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angola "Angola") and Mozambique.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-162)

Culture, language and identity
------------------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=White_Zimbabweans&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Culture, language and identity")]

Like other white diaspora in Africa who inherited European cultural dynamics from early settlers, many English-speaking white Rhodesians and Zimbabweans inherited social attitudes and mannerisms from British culture before developing their own distinct image and society with each generation. Post-World War II Rhodesian White settlers were considered different in character from earlier Rhodesian settlers and those from other British colonies. In [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"), settlers were perceived to be drawn from "the officer class" and from the British [landowning class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landed_gentry "Landed gentry"). By contrast, settlers in Rhodesia after the Second World War were perceived as being drawn from lower social strata and were treated accordingly by the British authorities. As White Zimbabwean author [Peter Godwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Godwin "Peter Godwin") wrote in _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_, "Foreign Office mandarins dismissed Rhodesians as lower middle class, no more than provincial clerks and artisans, the lowly NCOs of empire."[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-auto-34)

White Zimbabweans also developed a form of [Zimbabwean English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwean_English "Zimbabwean English") dialect and accent over time. Traditionally, this was influenced by [British English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_English "British English") with a smaller degree of Afrikaans influence, but White Zimbabweans have also adopted and integrated phrases and slang from native Bantu [Shona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shona_language "Shona language") and [Ndebele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ndebele_language_(Zimbabwe) "Ndebele language (Zimbabwe)") languages into parlance.[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-:0-163) British [sociolinguistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociolinguistics "Sociolinguistics") scholar [Peter Trudgill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Trudgill "Peter Trudgill") wrote that the white Rhodesian and later Zimbabwean accent evolved with the inclusion of terms and dialects used by both black and white communities.[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-164)[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-165) Citing his own family as an example, Peter Godwin described the White Zimbabwean accent as part of "a tiny subset of Anglo African accents" which blends influence from Afrikaans and [received pronunciation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Received_pronunciation "Received pronunciation") British-English.[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-166)

### Arts and entertainment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=White_Zimbabweans&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Arts and entertainment")]

Several cultural organisations existed during White-minority rule that mainly served the interests of the community. These included [The National Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Gallery_of_Zimbabwe "National Gallery of Zimbabwe"), The National Arts Foundation and the Salisbury Arts Council.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-CIM-167)

Artistic expression often portrays "the melancholy White exile" from Zimbabwe who secretly longs to return home.[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-168)

[Gertrude Page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gertrude_Page "Gertrude Page")'s Rhodesia novels were all written between the years 1907 and 1922.[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-ger-169) These novels included _[Love in the Wilderness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love\_in\_the\_Wilderness\_(novel) "Love in the Wilderness (novel)")_ (1907), _[The Edge O' Beyond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Edge\_O%27\_Beyond "The Edge O' Beyond")_ (1908) and _[The Pathway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Pathway\_(novel) "The Pathway (novel)")_ (1914).[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-ger-169) In _The Rhodesian_ (1914), Page writes admiringly of agricultural productivity and colonial settlement in her "empty" Rhodesian landscapes: "The Valley of Ruins no longer lies alone and unheeded in the sunlight; and no longer do the hills look down upon rich plains left solely to ... idle pleasures."[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-ger-169) In the novel she imagines [Cecil Rhodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Rhodes "Cecil Rhodes") as "enslaved and enfolded" by the landscape, an "enchantress who bound men's souls for ever", and wonders whether Rhodesia had been "wife and child" to him, in his solitude, thus implying that Page imagines Rhodes as a husband and father to the nation.[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-ger-169)[Cynthia Stockley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cynthia_Stockley "Cynthia Stockley"), the South African-born novelist, lived in Rhodesia and set several of her novels there such as _Virginia of the Rhodesians_ (1903) and _[The Claw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Claw\_(novel) "The Claw (novel)")_ (1911). As with Page, Stockley's heroes are heavily impacted by the powerful African landscape: "Africa has kissed him on the mouth and he will not leave her."[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-ger-169) In _The Claw_, she wrote of the country's empty landscapes that allowed for both personal freedom and expansion of the soul: "The world seemed filled with gracious dimness and made up of illimitable space. An indescribable feeling of happy freedom filled my heart. It seemed to me that the lungs of my soul drew breath and expanded as they had never done in any land before."[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-ger-169) Although Stockley shows a commitment to Rhodesian patriotism in her novels, her nationalism shifted towards [Union with South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1922_Southern_Rhodesian_government_referendum "1922 Southern Rhodesian government referendum") in _Tagati_ (1930).[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-ger-169)

[![Image 8: Woman with dark hair pulled back smiles while leaning against a windowsill, with a city and building in the background](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/DorisLessing1984.jpg/250px-DorisLessing1984.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:DorisLessing1984.jpg)

Author [Doris Lessing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doris_Lessing "Doris Lessing") in 1984

[Doris Lessing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doris_Lessing "Doris Lessing") (1919–2013) was awarded the [2007 Nobel Prize in Literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "2007 Nobel Prize in Literature"), becoming the second White African woman to win a [Nobel Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize "Nobel Prize"), after [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa")'s [Nadine Gordimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadine_Gordimer "Nadine Gordimer") in [1991](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "1991 Nobel Prize in Literature"). Her earlier poetry was published in the regular publication, _New Rhodesia_ (1938–1954), which published lively commentary affairs.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-degrut-170) Her debut novel, _[The Grass Is Singing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Grass\_Is\_Singing "The Grass Is Singing")_ (1950), about a relationship between a White woman and a Black man, is set in Southern Rhodesia of the late 1940s. The novel begins with a newspaper announcement of a White woman's murder on the veld: "The newspaper did not say much. People all over the country must have glanced at the paragraph with its sensational heading and felt a little spurt of anger mingled with what was almost satisfaction, as if some belief had been confirmed, as if something had happened which could only have been expected. When natives steal, murder or rape, that is the feeling white people have."[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-171)[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-172)

A number of White writers in the country had their poetry published by the Poetry Society of Rhodesia (founded in 1950). In 1952, the society's journal appeared as the _Poetry Review Salisbury_, before becoming _Rhodesian Poetry_.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-degrut-170)[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-poetry78-173) The South African writer [Alan Paton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Paton "Alan Paton") was a chairman of the society in the 1970s.[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-174) It appeared sometimes annually and sometimes biennially until independence in 1980.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-degrut-170) In the 1970s, it published new material as well as well-received poetry that had been published elsewhere in the country in the preceding two years.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-degrut-170) Many of these poems came from _Two Tone_, a quarterly publication that aimed to publish both Black and White writers. The founders, Phillipa Berlyn and Olive Robertson, were acolytes of the [Rhodesia Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia_Front "Rhodesia Front").[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-degrut-170) Berlyn held the belief that an independent Rhodesia would need to accommodate both Black and White citizens, and her quarterly could be an outlet where poets from different races could listen to one another.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-degrut-170) Once the [Rhodesian Bush War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Bush_War "Rhodesian Bush War") came to the forefront in 1972 and emigration increased, White poets became less confident in expressing their own identity, and more frequently the poems appearing in _Two Tone_ and _Rhodesian Poetry_ were about the experiences of war.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-degrut-170)[John Eppel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Eppel "John Eppel")[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-175)[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-176) was conscripted repeatedly during the final years of the war and in his poem "Spoils of War", he recalls looking at the bodies of guerrillas killed during a contact:[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-degrut-170)

> Sarge tells me to save my tears
> 
>  for the civilians these gooks have slaughtered.
> 
>  But I am not thinking of them, and I
> 
>  cannot explain that I am being purged
> 
>  of my Rhodesianism. That ugly
> 
>  word with its jagged edge is opening
> 
>  me. . . . I move to the past tense.

[Colin Style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Style "Colin Style"), a contributor to both _Two Tone_ and _Rhodesia Poetry_, was awarded the [Ingrid Jonker Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingrid_Jonker_Prize "Ingrid Jonker Prize") for best published collection in English in Southern Africa, 1977 with _Baobab Street_ (1977).[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-177)[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-rhodes-178) He wrote with unashamed nostalgia for his native country's [veld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veld "Veld"), its disappearance among new building developments and for Rhodesia itself. In "The Cemetery," the life and culture of a Rhodesia that will become a memory are presented as detached from the present as a San rock painting:[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-degrut-170)

> The soil is fine:
> 
>  it mingles with my sweat and stains red in my sandal,
> 
>  muddy itching ochre seeping into mind
> 
>  while in their crevices and caves the rock-imprinted impala
> 
>  restlessly stir.

[N. H. Brettell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N._H._Brettell "N. H. Brettell") was also a significant White poet in the country since publishing _Bronze Frieze: Poems Mostly Rhodesian_ (1950). In a 1978 academic essay on Rhodesian poetry, Graham Robin wrote that "Brettell puts into words the halting stupefaction of the exile in such a new and strange land. At last Rhodesia has a poet possessed by his country; but amazed, almost reluctantly possessed."[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-poetry78-173) Brettell also befriended the poet, short story writer and [Anglican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican "Anglican") priest, [Arthur Shearly Cripps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Shearly_Cripps "Arthur Shearly Cripps"). Cripps was critical of the [British South Africa Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_South_Africa_Company "British South Africa Company") and settler rule.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-degrut-170) He was the most widely represented writer in _Rhodesian Verse, 1888–1938_, the first anthology of Rhodesian poetry (edited by John Snelling).[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-degrut-170) In the post-war period and in his final years, Cripps published poetry in _Labour Front_, which provided a platform for White radicalism.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-degrut-170) Left-leaning White writers also wrote for the _Central African Examiner_ (1957–1965), where writers engaged with race, statehood and universal suffrage. The poetry was often satiric, subverting the political ideology and claims of the federal and Southern Rhodesian establishment.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-degrut-170) The publication ceased publication in 1965 due to the censorship laws put in place in the wake of [Rhodesia's Unilateral Declaration of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence "Rhodesia's Unilateral Declaration of Independence").[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-degrut-170) Hundreds of mostly partisan novels were also published in the UDI era of the 1960s and 1970s by White writers in the country supporting the Smith government.[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-rod-179)

In the final years of UDI Rhodesia, Rhodesian poetry that encompassed the work of both Black and White writers was seen as inappropriate by many Black writers.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-degrut-170) In 1978, Kizito Muchemwa edited _Zimbabwean Poetry in English: An Anthology_, a collection that only contained the work of Black writers.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-degrut-170) The use of Zimbabwean rather than Rhodesian as a term of identity was regarded as subversive at the time.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-degrut-170)

Writer [Alexander McCall Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_McCall_Smith "Alexander McCall Smith")

[Lauren Liebenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lauren_Liebenberg "Lauren Liebenberg") centred her debut novel, _The Voluptuous Delights of Peanut Butter and Jam_, on a Rhodesian farm in 1978. It was nominated for the [Orange Prize for Fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orange_Prize_for_Fiction "Orange Prize for Fiction") in 2008. Liebenberg drew upon some of her own experiences as a child growing up in war-torn Rhodesia.[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-180)[Alexander McCall Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_McCall_Smith "Alexander McCall Smith"), who was born and brought up in Southern Rhodesia, has also enjoyed notable success. In particular, he is known as the creator of the Africa-inspired series _[The No. 1 Ladies' Detective Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_No.\_1\_Ladies%27\_Detective\_Agency "The No. 1 Ladies' Detective Agency")_, set in neighbouring Botswana.[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-181)

[![Image 10: A man with light gray hair and graying stubble wears a dark top in a close-up](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/14/Peter_Godwin_head_shot.jpg/250px-Peter_Godwin_head_shot.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Peter_Godwin_head_shot.jpg)

Writer [Peter Godwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Godwin "Peter Godwin")

Uncritical accounts of White-minority rule in the country formed part of the teaching syllabi recommended by the Rhodesian Ministry of Education in the 1960s. White schoolchildren read _A Child's History of Rhodesia_ (1925) by Myfanwy Williams and _First Steps in Civilising Rhodesia_ (1940) by Jeannie M. Boogie.[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-rod-179)

[Peter Godwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Godwin_(writer) "Peter Godwin (writer)"), who was born in Salisbury (now [Harare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harare "Harare")) in 1957 to English and Polish parents, has written several books with a Zimbabwean background, including _Rhodesians Never Die_ (1984), _Mukiwa: A White Boy in Africa_ (1996), _[When a Crocodile Eats the Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/When\_a\_Crocodile\_Eats\_the\_Sun "When a Crocodile Eats the Sun")_ (2007) and _The Fear: Robert Mugabe and the Martyrdom of Zimbabwe_ (2011). The theme of these books is the impact of political change in Zimbabwe on the country's White community. His writing has been influenced by the death of one of his sisters in a "[friendly fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friendly_fire "Friendly fire")" incident during the Bush War in the 1970s. [Alexandra Fuller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandra_Fuller "Alexandra Fuller") wrote of her childhood in the 1970s on a Rhodesian farm in the memoir _[Don't Let's Go to the Dogs Tonight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don%27t\_Let%27s\_Go\_to\_the\_Dogs\_Tonight "Don't Let's Go to the Dogs Tonight")_ (2002).[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-fuller-182) For Fuller, the land is gendered female: "In Rhodesia we are born and then the umbilical cord of each child is sewn straight from the mother into the ground, where it takes root and grows. Pulling away from the ground causes death by suffocation, starvation. That's what the people of this land believe."[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-fuller-182)

[Graham Boynton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graham_Boynton "Graham Boynton"), who was raised in [Bulawayo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulawayo "Bulawayo"), wrote _Last Days in Cloud Cuckooland_ (1997), covering the twilight years of White rule in southern Africa and carried extensive interviews with the two major White political protagonists, Ian Smith and Sir Garfield Todd.[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-183) The late [Heidi Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heidi_Holland "Heidi Holland") met [Robert Mugabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe "Robert Mugabe") at a secret dinner, and in 2007 she was one of the few White journalists to be granted an in-depth interview with the president. Holland wrote about her experiences with Mugabe in _Dinner with Mugabe_ (2008).[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-184)[Douglas Rogers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Rogers_(writer) "Douglas Rogers (writer)") chronicled his parents' struggle to hold onto their game farm and backpackers resort in _The Last Resort_ (2009).[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-185)[Lauren St John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lauren_St_John "Lauren St John"), best known for her children's novels, wrote the memoir, _Rainbow's End: A Memoir of Childhood, War and an African Farm_. St John writes about her childhood home in then Rhodesia, Rainbow's End, where the previous family had been murdered. Her account explores growing up during the civil war in the 1970s and on life in a newly independent Zimbabwe.[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-186)[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-187)

"[God Save the Queen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God_Save_the_Queen "God Save the Queen")" was dropped as the [national anthem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_anthem "National anthem") when Rhodesia became a republic in 1970. In 1974, "[Ode to Joy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ode_to_Joy "Ode to Joy")" from [Beethoven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_van_Beethoven "Ludwig van Beethoven")'s [Ninth Symphony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._9_(Beethoven) "Symphony No. 9 (Beethoven)") became the tune for the new national anthem, "[Rise, O Voices of Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rise,_O_Voices_of_Rhodesia "Rise, O Voices of Rhodesia")".[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-188) Mary Bloom, a local woman provided the lyrics for the anthem.[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-189) Patriotic folk songs were particularly popular amongst the White community during the [Rhodesian Bush War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Bush_War "Rhodesian Bush War"). A leading musical figure was [Clem Tholet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clem_Tholet "Clem Tholet"), who married [Ian Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Smith "Ian Smith")'s stepdaughter Jean Smith in 1967. Tholet became famous for patriotic anthems such as "[Rhodesians Never Die](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesians_Never_Die "Rhodesians Never Die")", and he enjoyed gold status (for over 60,000 sales) with his first album, _Songs of Love & War_,[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-190) recorded at [Shed Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shed_Studios "Shed Studios"). Another popular folk singer was [Northern Rhodesian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Rhodesia "Northern Rhodesia")-born [John Edmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edmond "John Edmond"), a former soldier of the (Southern) [Rhodesian Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Army "Rhodesian Army"), who also enjoyed considerable success during the [Rhodesian Bush War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Bush_War "Rhodesian Bush War"). He had hits with patriotic folk songs such as "[The U.D.I. Song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_U.D.I._Song "The U.D.I. Song")" from his popular _Troopiesongs_ album.[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-191) Rhodesian Premier Ian Smith was criticised for singing the Afrikaans folk song, "Bobbe jaan Klim die Berg" ("The Baboon Climbs the Mountain") at an election rally in 1970 in Salisbury (Harare).[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-192)

Simon Attwell is a Zimbabwean band member of the popular South African group [Freshlyground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freshlyground "Freshlyground"), playing the flute, mbira, sax, and harmonica.[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-193) Freshlyground combines both African and European musical traditions,[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-194) and they participated in the 2008 HIFA. Gemma Griffifths, a singer and Harare native based in Cape Town, has been profiled by the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC").[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-195)

Concert pianist Manuel Bagorro is the founder and artistic director of [Harare International Festival of the Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harare_International_Festival_of_the_Arts "Harare International Festival of the Arts"). First held in 1999, the Festival was most recently held in April 2008, and was successful in attracting attention to the arts in Zimbabwe at a difficult time.[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-196)

The jazz composer, bandleader, and trombonist Mike Gibbs was born in Salisbury, Southern Rhodesia. Other internationally successful artists born there include the [Royal Ballet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Ballet "Royal Ballet")[prima ballerina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prima_ballerina "Prima ballerina")[Dame Merle Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dame_Merle_Park "Dame Merle Park") and actress [Susan Burnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Burnet "Susan Burnet"), whose grandfather was one of the country's first White settlers.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Theatre was immensely popular across African colonies amongst bourgeoise White residents, often seeking the culture of European metropoles. The construction of larger theatres boomed in the twentieth century in colonies most populated by White people, such as [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"), Southern Rhodesia and the copper belt of Northern Rhodesia. 'Little theatres' were also popular; often, they were part of large sporting venues, [gymkhana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gymkhana "Gymkhana") and turf clubs. In 1910, one author remarked on the popularity of theatre amongst Southern Rhodesia's White population: "the local population must have spent a considerable amount on theatre seats. Fifteen professional companies went on tour that year."[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-197) Theatres in Southern African colonies were usually situated next to a railway line, and the premier European dramatic performance in then Southern Rhodesia took place in the southern region of Bulawayo. The development of rail infrastructure allowed the involvement of entertainers from neighbouring South Africa.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-CIM-167)

The National Theatre Organisation, formerly The National Theatre Foundation, focussed on [Euro-centric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro-centric "Euro-centric") theatre productions. These included plays such as _[A Midsummer Night's Dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Midsummer\_Night%27s\_Dream "A Midsummer Night's Dream")_ and _No Sex Please, We're British_.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-CIM-167)

In 1960, television was introduced into the then Southern Rhodesia, as [Rhodesia Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia_Television "Rhodesia Television"). It was the first such service in the region, as South Africa did not introduce television until 1976, due to the potential ideological conflicts that it posed. The Rhodesian Broadcasting Corporation took over from Rhodesia Television (RTV) as RBCTV in 1976. As previously, this was a commercial service carrying advertising, although there was also a [television licence fee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_licence_fee "Television licence fee"). Television reception was confined mainly to the large cities, and the majority of television personalities and viewers were from the White minority. Both RTV and RBC used the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC") as a model, in that a government department was not responsible for it, but instead, a board of governors (selected by Ian Smith) were.[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-198) Popular television shows included _Kwizzkids_, _Frankly Partridge_ and _Music Time_.[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-199) Possibly the best-known Director of the RBC was Dr. [Harvey Ward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Ward_(director-general) "Harvey Ward (director-general)"). Prior to the introduction of television, RBC had developed a successful radio network, which continued. By 1978, three top White executives had fled overseas, including Dr. Ward, of whom it was said "probably more than any other person, became identified with the right-wing bias on Rhodesia's radio and TV networks."[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-200) The RBC was later succeeded by the Zimbabwe Rhodesia Corporation, and later in its present form as the [Zimbabwe Broadcasting Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_Broadcasting_Corporation "Zimbabwe Broadcasting Corporation"). The character Horace Von Khute from the British television series _[Fonejacker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fonejacker "Fonejacker")_ is a Rhodesian who works for the police in intercepting a Ugandan bank scammer.

Georgina Godwin, sister of author Peter Godwin, became a well-known broadcast journalist in Zimbabwe, presenting a [breakfast television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakfast_television "Breakfast television") show and hosting a prime time radio show on the state broadcaster, [Zimbabwe Broadcasting Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_Broadcasting_Corporation "Zimbabwe Broadcasting Corporation") until her departure from the country in 2001.[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-201) She was also a founder of [SW Radio Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SW_Radio_Africa "SW Radio Africa"), a station based in London with the purpose of broadcasting independently of Zimbabwean state interference.[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-Radio_Free_Zimbabwe-202) She is books editor for [Monocle Radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monocle_Radio "Monocle Radio") and presenter of the in-depth author interview show _Meet the Writers_ on the station.[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-203)

Doris Lessing's Southern Rhodesia novel _[The Grass is Singing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Grass\_is\_Singing "The Grass is Singing")_ was adapted into a film by the White Zimbabwean director, [Michael Raeburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Raeburn "Michael Raeburn") and released in 1980. Despite the majority of the original novel taking place in then Southern Rhodesia and earlier scenes in South Africa, the adaptation was filmed in [Zambia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambia "Zambia") and [Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden "Sweden"). The film starred [Karen Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karen_Black "Karen Black") and [John Thaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Thaw "John Thaw") as the poverty-stricken Ehite farming couple Mary and Dick Turner, and [John Kani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kani "John Kani") as the Black [houseboy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houseboy "Houseboy") and love-interest of Mary Turner. The film is also known as _Gräset Sjunger_ (Swedish) and _Killing Heat_.[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-204)

The 1980 film _[Shamwari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shamwari\_(film) "Shamwari (film)")_, also known as _Chain Gang Killings_ in the United States, is an [action thriller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_thriller "Action thriller") about two escaped prisoners, one Black, one White and their developing friendship. The film was set and filmed in Rhodesia, starring several local White actors, such as [Tamara Franke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamara_Franke "Tamara Franke") in the role of Tracy.[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-205) Four years later, Franke had a major role in _[Go for Gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Go\_for\_Gold\_(film) "Go for Gold (film)")_.[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-206)

The documentary film _[Mugabe and the White African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugabe\_and\_the\_White\_African "Mugabe and the White African")_ was released to acclaim in 2009. It deals with a White Zimbabwean farming family working against Mugabe's draconian land reform policies.[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-207)

In _[Blood Diamond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood\_Diamond\_(film) "Blood Diamond (film)")_ (2006), [Leonard DiCaprio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_DiCaprio "Leonard DiCaprio") plays Danny Archer, an ex-[mercenary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercenary "Mercenary"), diamond-smuggler and self-proclaimed "Rhodesian", whose parents were murdered on their farm by rebels. The adventure drama film is set in 1999 during the [Sierra Leone Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_Leone_Civil_War "Sierra Leone Civil War").[[207]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-208) In _[The Interpreter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Interpreter\_(2005\_film) "The Interpreter (2005 film)")_ (2005) by [Sydney Pollack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Pollack "Sydney Pollack"), [Nicole Kidman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicole_Kidman "Nicole Kidman") plays the lead role of Silvia Broome, a White African and New York-based United Nations interpreter raised in the fictional African republic of Matobo under the rule of an authoritarian leader. Matobo is widely considered to be symbolic of Zimbabwe and the film contains parallels between Mugabe and Matobo's fictional dictator.[[208]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-209)[[209]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-210)

[Miss Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miss_Rhodesia "Miss Rhodesia") was the national beauty pageant of Rhodesia and its antecedents. Each year many local White women competed in the competition and it debuted in [Miss World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miss_World "Miss World") in 1959. Rhodesia participated in [Miss World 1965](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miss_World_1965 "Miss World 1965"), with Lesley Bunting representing the country only days after Rhodesia's Unilateral Declaration of Independence.[[210]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-211) However, the country was excluded from the competition from 1966 onwards. Beverley Donald Davy, the mother of [Chelsy Davy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsy_Davy "Chelsy Davy"), was crowned the 1973 Miss Rhodesia.[[211]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-212) Only White women were crowned Miss Rhodesia between 1959 and 1976, with Connie Makaya becoming the first Black Miss Rhodesia in 1977.[[212]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-213) When Rhodesia transitioned to a majority democracy and became Zimbabwe in 1980, Miss Rhodesia became Miss Zimbabwe. In 2023, [Brooke Bruk-Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooke_Bruk-Jackson "Brooke Bruk-Jackson"), a White Zimbabwean woman was crowned [Miss Universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miss_Universe "Miss Universe") Zimbabwe.[[213]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-214)

[![Image 13: A group of women stand on a field celebrating with one on another's shoulders](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/RIAN_archive_556180_Women%27s_field_hockey_team_from_Zimbabwe.jpg/330px-RIAN_archive_556180_Women%27s_field_hockey_team_from_Zimbabwe.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:RIAN_archive_556180_Women%27s_field_hockey_team_from_Zimbabwe.jpg)

The all-White [Zimbabwean field hockey team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_women%27s_national_field_hockey_team "Zimbabwe women's national field hockey team") that [won gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_women%27s_national_field_hockey_team_at_the_1980_Summer_Olympics "Zimbabwe women's national field hockey team at the 1980 Summer Olympics") at the [1980 Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Summer_Olympics "1980 Summer Olympics")

Before 1980, Rhodesian representation in international sporting events was almost exclusively White. Zimbabwean participation in some international sporting events continued to be White-dominated until well into the 1990s. For example, no Black player was selected for the [Zimbabwean cricket team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwean_cricket_team "Zimbabwean cricket team") until 1995.[[214]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-215) Rally driver [Conrad Rautenbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conrad_Rautenbach "Conrad Rautenbach") (son of Billy) won the [FIA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIA "FIA") African Championship, scoring at the Dunlop Zimbabwe Challenge Rally in 2005 and 2006.[[215]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-216) An iconic event is the all-White Zimbabwean women's field hockey team, captained by [Ann Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ann_Grant "Ann Grant") (formerly Ann Fletcher) and [winning gold medals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_women%27s_national_field_hockey_team_at_the_1980_Summer_Olympics "Zimbabwe women's national field hockey team at the 1980 Summer Olympics") at the [Moscow Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow_Olympics "Moscow Olympics") in July 1980 (Ann Grant's brother, cricketer [Duncan Fletcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duncan_Fletcher "Duncan Fletcher"), later became manager of the England cricket team).

An exception to this trend during the 1960s and 1970s was in [association football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football"), where the [national team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_national_football_team "Zimbabwe national football team") was predominantly Black, with the notable exceptions of the White forward [Bobby Chalmers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Chalmers "Bobby Chalmers"), who captained the team during its unsuccessful attempt to [qualify](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1970_FIFA_World_Cup_qualification "1970 FIFA World Cup qualification") for the [1970 World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1970_FIFA_World_Cup "1970 FIFA World Cup"),[[216]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-217) and goalkeeper [Bruce Grobbelaar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Grobbelaar "Bruce Grobbelaar").

The professional swimmer, [Charlene, Princess of Monaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlene,_Princess_of_Monaco "Charlene, Princess of Monaco"), competed at the [2000 Sydney Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Sydney_Olympics "2000 Sydney Olympics"). She was born and raised in Bulawayo, before relocating with her family to South Africa in 1989 when she was twelve years old. However, she represented South Africa at professional sporting competitions.[[217]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-bbc1-218) Australian rugby union player [David Pocock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Pocock "David Pocock") is also a well-known Zimbabwean, having emigrated to Australia in 2002 at age 14.[[218]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-maley-219) Pocock would be elected an [Australian Senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Senate "Australian Senate") in [2022](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Australian_federal_election "2022 Australian federal election"). He would renounce his Zimbabwean citizenship to comply with [section 44(1)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Section_44_of_the_Constitution_of_Australia "Section 44 of the Constitution of Australia") of the [Australian Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Australia "Constitution of Australia"), which forbids parliamentarians from holding dual citizenship.[[219]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-220)

Involvement in Zimbabwean politics
----------------------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=White_Zimbabweans&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: Involvement in Zimbabwean politics")]

### Political and economic background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=White_Zimbabweans&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: Political and economic background")]

[![Image 14: Group of men in suits and ties, arranged in rows, with two portraits of men in circles above them](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/First_government_of_rhodesia.jpg/330px-First_government_of_rhodesia.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:First_government_of_rhodesia.jpg)

First government of [Southern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia "Southern Rhodesia") in 1923

During the UDI era, Rhodesia developed a siege economy as the means of withstanding UN sanctions. The country operated a strict system of exchange and import controls, while major export items were channelled through state trade agencies (such as 'the Grain Marketing Board'). This approach was continued until around 1990, at which time [International Monetary Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Monetary_Fund "International Monetary Fund") and [World Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Bank "World Bank") development funding was made conditional upon the adoption of economic liberalisation. In 1991, Zimbabwe adopted the ESAP (Economic Structural Adjustment Programme), which required privatisation, the removal of exchange and import controls, trade deregulation and the phasing out of export subsidies.[[220]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-221) Up until the time of independence, the economy relied mainly on the export of a narrow range of primary products, including tobacco, asbestos and gold. In the post-independence period, the world markets for all these products deteriorated, and it was hoped that the ESAP would facilitate diversification.[[221]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-222)

ESAP and its successor ZIMPREST (Zimbabwe Programme for Economic and Social Transformation) caused considerable economic turbulence.[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-223) Some sectors of the economy did benefit, but the immediate results included job losses, a rise in poverty, and a series of exchange rate crises. The associated economic downturn caused the budget deficit to rise, which put pressure on public services, and the means used to finance the budget deficit caused hyperinflation. These factors created a situation in which many bright and qualified Zimbabweans (both Black and White) had to look abroad for work opportunities.[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-224)

Zimbabwean politics since 1990 have therefore been conducted against a background of economic difficulty, with the manufacturing sector (in particular) being 'hollowed out'. However, some parts of the economy continue to perform well: the Zimbabwe stock exchange and property market have experienced minor booms, while outsiders are coming to invest in both mining and land operations.[[224]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-225)

In the period immediately after independence, some White political leaders (such as [Ian Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Smith "Ian Smith")) sought to maintain the identity of White Zimbabweans as a separate group. In particular, they wished to maintain a separate "white roll", maintaining the election of 20 seats in parliament reserved for White people; this was abolished in 1987. Despite this, a number of White Zimbabweans embraced the political changes, and many even joined Zanu-PF in the 1980s and 1990s: for example, [Timothy Stamps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_Stamps "Timothy Stamps") served as Minister of Health in the Zimbabwean government from 1986 to 2002.[[225]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-226)[Denis Norman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_Norman "Denis Norman") held several cabinet positions; [Minister of Agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Agriculture_(Zimbabwe) "Ministry of Agriculture (Zimbabwe)") (1980–1985, 1995–1997), [Minister of Transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Transport,_Communication_and_Infrastructural_Development_(Zimbabwe) "Ministry of Transport, Communication and Infrastructural Development (Zimbabwe)") (1990–1997) and [Minister of Power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Energy_and_Power_Development "Ministry of Energy and Power Development") (1992–1997).[[226]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-227)

### Wealthy Zimbabweans

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=White_Zimbabweans&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: Wealthy Zimbabweans")]

In the 2000s, an elite network of White businessmen and senior military officers became associated with a faction of ZANU-PF identified with [Emmerson Mnangagwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmerson_Mnangagwa "Emmerson Mnangagwa"), a former Security Minister and later Speaker of Parliament. Mnangagwa was described by reporters of the _[Daily News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily\_News\_(Harare) "Daily News (Harare)")_ as "the richest politician in Zimbabwe".[[227]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-228) He is believed to have favoured the early retirement of President Mugabe, and a conciliatory approach towards the regime's domestic opponents; this line has displeased other elements in ZANU-PF. In June 2006, [John Bredenkamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bredenkamp "John Bredenkamp") (a prominent former Mnangagwa associate) fled Zimbabwe in his private jet, after government investigations into the affairs of his Breco trading company were started.[[228]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-229) Bredenkamp returned to Zimbabwe in September 2006, after his passport was returned by court order.[[229]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-230)

In July 2002, 92 prominent Zimbabweans were subject to [EU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") "smart sanctions", intended to express disapproval of various Zimbabwe government policies. These persons were banned from the EU, and access to assets they own in the EU was frozen.[[230]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-231) Ninety-one of those on the blacklist were Black, and one was White: Dr. Timothy Stamps.

Many observers found the EU's treatment of Dr. Stamps to be curious, given that by July 2002 he was retired from active politics and a semi-invalid. In addition, Stamps was widely considered to be a highly dedicated doctor who had never been implicated in any form of wrongdoing.[[231]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-232) The same observers found it equally strange that the EU Commission did not include the wealthy White backers of Mugabe on the list.[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_][[232]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-233)

### Political representation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=White_Zimbabweans&action=edit&section=32 "Edit section: Political representation")]

[![Image 15: Estonian curling coach Nicole Strausak poses for a photo wearing an athletic style top with the Olympic rings displayed on it](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/2018-10-17_Boxing_lightweight_Boys%27_%E2%80%9360_kg_at_2018_Summer_Youth_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Victory_ceremony_%28Martin_Rulsch%29_2_%28cropped_3%29.jpg/250px-2018-10-17_Boxing_lightweight_Boys%27_%E2%80%9360_kg_at_2018_Summer_Youth_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Victory_ceremony_%28Martin_Rulsch%29_2_%28cropped_3%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2018-10-17_Boxing_lightweight_Boys%27_%E2%80%9360_kg_at_2018_Summer_Youth_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Victory_ceremony_(Martin_Rulsch)_2_(cropped_3).jpg)

Youth, sports and recreation minister (2018-2025) [Kirsty Coventry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirsty_Coventry "Kirsty Coventry")

[![Image 16: A man with short brown hair wearing a suit and tie smiles at the camera](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/David_Coltart.JPG/250px-David_Coltart.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:David_Coltart.JPG)

Bulawayo mayor [David Coltart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Coltart "David Coltart")

From around 1990 onwards, mainstream White opinion favoured opposition politics to that of Mugabe's ZANU party, who controlled the government.[[233]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-234) White Zimbabweans sought to vote for liberal economics, democracy and the rule of law. White people had lain low in the immediate post-independence period, but, in 1999 they recognised a common disquiet with the majority of people over ZANU excesses in government, and gave whites an opportunity to vote for an opposition, which initially grew out of the trade union movements who were enabling citizens to have a voice and vote with the majority of Zimbabweans.[[234]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-235) White Zimbabweans played a significant role in the campaign of the opposition MDC party, which almost won the election.[[235]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-236) Radical elements in the country perceived the MDC project to have been an attempt to restore a limited form of White minority rule, and this produced a violent backlash.[[236]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-237)[[237]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-238)

The late [Roy Bennett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Bennett_(politician) "Roy Bennett (politician)"), a White farmer forced off his coffee plantation after it was overrun by radical militants and then expropriated, won a strong victory in the Chimanimani constituency (adjoining the Mozambican border) in the [2000 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Zimbabwean_parliamentary_election "2000 Zimbabwean parliamentary election"). Bennett (a former [Conservative Alliance of Zimbabwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Alliance_of_Zimbabwe "Conservative Alliance of Zimbabwe") member) won his seat for the [Movement for Democratic Change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movement_for_Democratic_Change_(pre-2005) "Movement for Democratic Change (pre-2005)"), and was one of four White MDC constituency MPs elected in 2000.[[238]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-239)[[239]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-240) Bennett died in a [helicopter crash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Sapphire_Aviation_Bell_UH-1_crash "2018 Sapphire Aviation Bell UH-1 crash") in [Raton, New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raton,_New_Mexico "Raton, New Mexico"), United States in 2018.[[240]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-241)

Other White MPs elected in 2000 included [David Coltart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Coltart "David Coltart") (a prominent human rights lawyer and founding legal secretary of the MDC) and Michael Auret (a civil rights activist of long standing, who had opposed White minority rule in the 1970s). [Trudy Stevenson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trudy_Stevenson "Trudy Stevenson") was a White American who had lived in [Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda") until 1972, before fleeing from the regime of [Idi Amin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idi_Amin "Idi Amin").[[241]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-242) Stevenson served as the MDC's Secretary for Policy and Research before being elected to Parliament. In July 2006, after attending a political meeting in the Harare suburb of Mabvuku, Stevenson was attacked, suffering [panga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machete "Machete") wounds to the back of her neck and head. The MDC leadership immediately claimed that the attack was carried out by ZANU militants; however, while recovering in hospital, the MP for Harare North positively identified her assailants as members of a rival faction of the MDC. This incident illustrates the violent and faction-ridden nature of Zimbabwean politics.[[242]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-243) Zimbabwean politicians routinely accuse each other of murder, theft, electoral fraud, conspiracy and treason; it is often difficult to know the truth of such stories.[[243]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-244)[Eddie Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Cross "Eddie Cross") was also elected to parliament in 2000 before retiring from politics in 2018.[[244]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-245)[[245]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-246) Cross, a leading economist, served as the MDC's Economic Secretary and shadow finance minister.[[246]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-247) In the [Parliamentary and Presidential elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwean_parliamentary_election,_2008 "Zimbabwean parliamentary election, 2008"), Cross, and Coltart were re-elected to their seats and a White Zimbabwean farmer, [Iain Kay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iain_Kay "Iain Kay") took the seat of [Marondera Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marondera_Central "Marondera Central").[[247]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-248)[[248]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-249) Stevenson lost her seat in Mount Pleasant, Harare.[[249]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-250) Stevenson served as Zimbabwe's ambassador to [Senegal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senegal "Senegal") from 2009 until her death in 2019.[[250]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-251)

[Kirsty Coventry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirsty_Coventry "Kirsty Coventry") was [Minister of Youth, Sport, Arts and Recreation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Youth,_Sport,_Arts_and_Recreation_(Zimbabwe) "Ministry of Youth, Sport, Arts and Recreation (Zimbabwe)") from 2018 to 2025.[[251]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-252)[[252]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans#cite_note-253)
